sources.title: NCERT: Kings, Farmers and Towns, sections 2.2 and 3
sources.note: Official IIT Kanpur SATHEE reproduction of NCERT Class XII. Indexed original read, direct fetch failed. Section 2.2 explains productive agriculture, iron, elephants, waterways and capitals; section 3 dates Chandragupta circa 321 BCE. Section 2.2 says fourth century for capital shift, while the Pataliputra box says fifth: public text does not choose an exact capital-transfer date.

sources.title: NCERT: Kingdoms, Kings and an Early Republic
sources.note: Indexed official reproduction read: Taxes; Changes in agriculture; A closer look, Magadha. General mahajanapada agriculture and taxation are marked as regional context, not an excavated household survey.

sources.title: IGNOU, BHIC-101, Unit 15: pre-Mauryan Magadha and Mauryan emergence
sources.note: Direct PDF unavailable; indexed original explicitly states that Indian and Classical sources agree Chandragupta overthrew the last Nanda and occupied Pataliputra, linking this to accession around 321 BCE. Only that narrow transition is cited here.

sources.title: Archaeological Survey of India, Patna Circle: Rajgir monuments
sources.note: Official indexed entries 40 to 42 read. Entry 40 describes mortarless stone-boulder walls and sixth to fifth century BCE dating. Harding challenges a single continuous defensive interpretation; both positions are made explicit. Do not reproduce the unsupported superlative first capital city of India.

sources.title: Robert Harding, Rajgir and Its Hinterland, 2003
sources.note: Cambridge doctoral field survey. Indexed original repository abstract read, conclusions 1, 2, 6, 7, 8 and 10. Full PDF access failed; claims are limited to the explicit abstract. This is a named research interpretation, not an assertion that every archaeologist agrees.

sources.title: e-PG Pathshala: Imperial Punch Marked Coins, Magadha-Maurya Coinage
sources.note: Indexed original teaching module, summary page 6: five separately struck symbols; 3.4 gram karshapana standard; multiple coin series and expansion under Mauryas. Direct fetch returns unauthorized. Supplement from the same module is one work for attribution.

sources.title: e-PG Pathshala: Magadha-Maurya Coinage, timeline and glossary
sources.note: Indexed original sections 5.2 and 5.3: fourth to second century BCE broad timeline; coins lack ruler names, so exact reign assignment uncertain. Combined with the teaching text under one work limit.

sources.title: Surface elemental and structural analysis of ancient Indian punch-marked coins, Scientific Reports, 2024
sources.note: Original research read directly. Historical background and methodology specify nine specimens in the Numismatic Society of India collection, BHU; acquisition and exact provenance unknown. XRD/XPS results show silver dominance and other elements; public paragraph avoids treating surface readings as a complete state budget or assigning every specimen to pre-Mauryan Magadha.

sources.title: Samannaphala Sutta, Digha Nikaya 2, translated by Thanissaro Bhikkhu
sources.note: Read directly: opening at Rajagaha and Jivaka mango grove; rival teachers; The King’s Question lists occupations and relatives supported by earnings. Religious dialogue is evidence of transmitted literary representations, not a dated verbatim court transcript. All DN passages and the Pali witness are conservatively treated as one work for the 200-word budget.

sources.title: Sigalovada Sutta, Digha Nikaya 31, translated by Narada Thera
sources.note: Read directly: Rajagaha setting; six-direction relationships; parents teach a profession, children support parents, teachers ensure understanding. Prescriptive household ideals, not universal practice or public-school statistics.

sources.title: SuttaCentral, Digha Nikaya 2: Pali root text
sources.note: Direct Pali data read, segment dn2:2.5 includes rājā māgadho ajātasattu vedehiputto after Evaṁ vutte. Public excerpt selects the three-word royal identification, matched with the English translation’s identification of King Ajatasattu of Magadha. Modern Roman transcription of a transmitted Pali text, not an original pre-Mauryan inscription or contemporary manuscript.

sources.title: Vinaya, Mahavagga VIII: the Jivaka narrative
sources.note: Full translated primary text read directly. Opening Rajagaha narrative; Taxila apprenticeship for seven years and plant-finding exercise; return to Rajagaha and royal medicine. Religious biography is clearly distinguished from a clinical report. Combined with nursing excerpt as one Mahavagga VIII work.

sources.title: Mahavagga 8.26: The Monk with Dysentery, translated by Thanissaro Bhikkhu
sources.note: Direct reading of 8.26.1 to 8. Nurses wash a patient, remove waste and comfort the ill; community responsibility specified. Passage is wider Buddhist monastic context, not a claimed Magadhan hospital excavation or sanitation census.

sources.title: Human History Map: imported Magadha border geometry
sources.note: Locally decoded source TopoJSON in identities.json. Two additional Magadha geometries for 400 to 323 BCE lie at roughly 25 E, 65 N and 35 E, 65 N. They are erroneous northern European outliers. The main interval progresses from eastern India to a very broad subcontinental outline; exact territorial boundaries are not independently validated.

proposedOverrides.name: Magadha
proposedOverrides.summary: Magadha’s growing kingdom became the heartland of the Mauryan Empire.

batchIdentityNotes.decision: A distinct early Magadha narrative; no association with magadha-200 or the existing Maurya card.
batchIdentityNotes.mapWindow: Approximately 500 to 300 BCE. Two erroneous northern European polygons in the 400 to 323 BCE snapshot are explicitly flagged in public copy. No border files changed.
batchIdentityNotes.periodBasis: Approximate interpretive phases, with the last transition dated circa 321 BCE after NCERT and IGNOU, not forced to the existing Maurya index start of 322 BCE.
batchIdentityNotes.writing: Transmitted Pali in verified modern Roman transcription; no contemporary autograph or securely identified pre-Mauryan royal inscription claimed.
batchIdentityNotes.limits: Archaeological interpretations are attributed; medical stories and household prescriptions are literary evidence. No pre-Mauryan household toilet or hospital excavation could be verified in this bounded search, so none is invented.
